How a day works

  1. Open today's set. Start the Reading & Writing timer (12 minutes), then the Math timer (19 minutes). Tap an answer to choose it.
  2. Tap Check my answers. The set marks itself, shows the right answers, and opens the key with a reason for each one.
  3. Log every miss. Find its pattern in the Pattern Bank and write it in the error log. This is where the score goes up.
  4. Look at Progress. Each day's score lands on the chart. The dashed line is the pace a 1400 needs.

Jump to

Scores and ticks are saved in this browser on this device. Use the same browser each day, and do not clear its site data.

Daily

Daily Practice

One hour a day from Thursday 8 October to Friday 6 November. Tap an answer, press Check my answers, and the set marks itself and saves the score to the Progress page. There are 1199 questions in all.

What each day holds

PartQuestionsTimeWhat it is for
Hour set2212 min R&W, 19 min Math, then reviewThe core. This is the score that is tracked.
Today's words and Desmos drill6 words, 1 drill5 minVocabulary and calculator speed
Pattern drill610 minThe question types the SAT repeats most: data tables, models, formulas, study design
Extra set1320 minMore volume when there is time

The one hour. Retry due error-log questions for 5 minutes. Do the hour set against the two timers. Check, read the key for every miss, and log it. Finish with the words and the drill. The Pattern drill and Extra set are for days with more time.

Three levels. Days 1 to 8 are Foundation. Days 9 to 18 are Core. Days 19 to 29 are Hard mix. Day 30 is a short warm-up, then rest.

62

Pattern Bank

The SAT asks the same 62 kinds of question again and again. Learn to name the pattern in the first five seconds and the method follows. Every daily Pattern drill is built from these.

Reading & Writing: 21 patterns

PatternHow to spot itThe move
Words in contextA blank in a sentence and four single wordsCover the choices. Predict your own word from the clue, then match it. Decide positive or negative first if stuck.
Main idea“Which choice best states the main idea”Summarize in eight words. Pick the choice that covers the whole text. Drop anything that is only one detail.
Detail“According to the text”Find the sentence. The answer is that sentence in other words.
Logical completionThe text ends in a blankFind the two facts set side by side. The answer joins them with the smallest possible step.
Support a claim“Would most directly support”Split the claim into its parts. The right finding matches every part.
Weaken a claim“Would most weaken”Look for the choice that breaks the cause, or shows the same result without it.
Data from a tableA table or graph with a claimRead the claim first. A change needs two numbers. A comparison needs both groups.
Function of a sentence“Function of the underlined sentence”Label it with a verb: contrasts, explains, concedes, gives an example. Match the verb before the content.
Paired textsText 1 and Text 2One line for each author. Name the relationship. Prefer the qualified answer over total agreement or rejection.
Two full sentencesChoices differ only in punctuationSemicolon or period. A comma needs and, but or so. A comma alone is always wrong.
Extra informationA phrase that could be lifted outTwo commas or two dashes, never one of each. Check with the removal test.
Name after a title“The physicist ______ discovered”No commas when the name tells you which one.
ColonA list or explanation followsThere must be a complete sentence before the colon. Never after “such as” or a verb.
Subject and verbChoices differ in singular or pluralCross out the “of the…” phrase. Match the real subject.
Verb tenseChoices differ in tenseFollow the time marker and the verbs around it.
Verb formChoices mix -ing, “to” and full verbsEvery sentence needs exactly one real main verb.
Its, their, whoseChoices are sound-alikesSay “it is” or “they are”. If it fails, use the form without the apostrophe.
Possessive pluralChoices move the apostropheAsk whether anything is owned, then whether there is one owner or several.
Opening modifierThe sentence starts with a describing phraseThe person or thing doing it must come right after the comma.
TransitionA blank between two sentencesDecide the link before looking: same direction, opposite, cause, example. Two choices that mean the same are both wrong.
NotesBullet notes and a goalRead only the goal. Pick the choice that does that job. Every choice is true.

Math: 41 patterns

PatternHow to spot itThe move
Asks for an expressionThe question wants 3x + 1, not xWrite what is asked before solving. Check it before clicking.
System asking for x + yTwo equations, a combined answerAdd or subtract the equations first. The answer often appears at once.
No solution or infinitely manyA system or equation with a constant kMatch the ratios of the coefficients. Same slope, different constant means none.
Line through two pointsTwo points givenSlope first, then substitute one point for the intercept.
Meaning of a number“What does 12 represent”Number beside the variable is the rate per unit. The lone number is the starting amount.
Build a linear modelA story with a fixed part and a rateFixed amount plus rate times the variable. Check the sign for draining or spending.
Break-even and budgetsTwo plans, or “at most” and “at least”Write the inequality. Test the boundary whole number.
Parallel and perpendicularA line related to anotherEqual slopes, or flip the fraction and change the sign.
Absolute valueBars around an expressionTwo cases: equals c or equals -c.
Quadratic rootsSolve a quadraticFactor, or graph in Desmos and click the x-intercepts.
Maximum or minimum“Greatest height”, “minimum value”x = -b/(2a), or click the turning point in Desmos. Check whether x or y is asked.
Number of solutions“How many real solutions”Discriminant: positive two, zero one, negative none.
One intersectionA line and parabola with a constant kSet equal, discriminant zero. Or use a Desmos slider.
Equivalent expression“Which is equivalent to”Expand or factor. Or put x = 2 into the original and each choice.
Exponent rulesPowers multiplied, divided or raisedAdd, subtract or multiply the exponents. A fraction exponent is a root.
Radical equationA square root with x insideSquare both sides, then test every answer in the original.
Factor of a polynomial“(x − a) is a factor”Then p(a) = 0. Substitute and solve.
Function inside a functionf(g(3))Work from the inside out.
Exponential model“Doubles every k years”, “grows by 5%”a(2)t/k, or a(1 ± r)t.
Meaning of 0.92An exponential with a base below 1The base is 1 minus the rate: an 8% decrease.
Rearranging a formula“Which gives h in terms of”Undo each operation in reverse order.
Percent changeFrom one value to another(new − old) / old.
Reverse percentA price after a discount or riseDivide by the multiplier. Never subtract the percent from the new price.
Two percents in a rowUp 20%, then down 20%Multiply the multipliers.
Mean with totalsA mean before and afterTotal = mean × count. Subtract the totals.
Median and outliersOne value changes a lotThe mean moves. The median usually does not.
Two-way table“Given that” or “of those who”That row or column becomes the new total.
Margin of errorA sample percent with ± mEstimate ± margin, and only for the population sampled.
Study design“Which conclusion is appropriate”Random sample lets you generalize. Random assignment lets you claim cause.
Line of best fitA scatterplot with an equationSubstitute for a prediction. The slope is the predicted change per unit.
Unit conversionMixed unitsMultiply by fractions equal to 1. Square the factor for area.
Similar trianglesShadows, nested trianglesSet up a proportion. Areas scale by the square.
Pythagorean triplesRight triangle with whole sides3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and their multiples.
Special right triangles45° or 30° and 60°x, x, x√2 or x, x√3, 2x.
Circle equationx2 + y2 with extra termsComplete the square, or type it into Desmos. The right side is r2.
Arc and sectorA central angleAngle / 360 of the circumference or the area.
sin and cossin x = cos yThe angles add to 90.
One trig ratio to anothertan A given, cos A askedDraw the triangle, label two sides, find the third.
Radiansπ in an angleMultiply by 180/π.
VolumeCylinder, cone, sphereUse the reference sheet. If lengths scale by k, volume scales by k3.
Angles and parallel linesA third line crossing two parallel linesOnly two angle sizes exist, and they add to 180.

How to use this page

  1. Before each daily set, read five rows.
  2. When she misses a question, find its pattern here and write the pattern name in the error log.
  3. By 24 October she should be able to name the pattern for every question in a set before solving it.

Guide

How to use this book

Follow the day-by-day plan in Book 1. It tells her which other book to open each day. Nothing here is meant to be read cover to cover.

Today (Thursday October 8)

  1. Print the Roadmap & Checklist and put the roadmap on her desk.
  2. Confirm her November 7 registration and test centre in her College Board account.
  3. Install Bluebook on the device she will use on test day.
  4. Take the diagnostic in Book 1 (44 minutes, timed), then mark it with the key.
  5. Print 10 copies of the error log from Book 7.

Tomorrow (Friday October 9)

Take Bluebook practice test 1 at 8:00 AM under the rules in Book 6. Do the five-step analysis the same afternoon. Her score decides which rows of the plan to lean on.

Book Open it How to use it

Rules that make it work

  • She works alone and timed. A parent's job is the schedule, the printing and the Friday error count, not explaining answers.
  • Answer keys stay covered. Each key sits at the end of its book. Scroll there only after finishing the set.
  • The error log is not optional. If time is short, cut new questions, never the log.
  • Adjust after each test. Strong domains skip their concept lessons. Weak ones get the first 20 minutes of the day.
  • Use official questions for volume. This book teaches the method. The College Board question bank and Bluebook supply the practice.

Roadmap & Checklist

30-Day 1400+ Roadmap

Target: 1400+ on Saturday, November 7, 2026. Aim for 700+ in each section. About 85 study hours in 30 days.

The three rules that produce the score

  1. Never lose an easy or medium question. Hard questions decide 750 vs 700. Easy ones decide 700 vs 620.
  2. Every wrong answer goes in the error log the same day and gets retried 3 days later.
  3. One official Bluebook full test every week, at 8:00 AM, under real conditions.

Every single day

The 30-day strategy

The plan spends hours where points are cheapest. Grammar rules and Algebra are learnable in days and cover a large share of the test. Hard reading inference improves slowly, so it gets steady practice, not cramming.

An honest note on the target. Thirty days typically moves a score by 80 to 150 points with disciplined work. If Test 1 on October 9 is 1250 or above, 1400 is a realistic goal. If it is below 1150, follow the same plan, but also register for December 5 (deadline November 20) as a second attempt.

Registration check. The regular registration deadline for November 7 is October 23. Confirm her seat and test center today.

Priority Area Why it comes first
1 Standard English Conventions (grammar, punctuation) About a quarter of R&W. Rule-based, so it is the fastest gain.
2 Algebra and Advanced Math About 70% of Math between them.
3 Transitions and notes questions Formulaic. Near 100% accuracy is achievable.
4 Desmos fluency Turns several hard questions into 30-second questions.
5 Words in context, inference, evidence Slower to improve. Daily short practice.
6 Geometry, trig, statistics About 30% of Math. Mostly formula recall.

Book 1

SAT 1400+ Strategy

What 1400+ requires

A 1400 needs roughly 85 to 90% accuracy in both sections. Every combination below works. Pick the one that matches her stronger section after Test 1.

R&W Math Total Who it suits
700 700 1400 Balanced
680 720 1400 Stronger in Math (common for CBSE Science students)
660 740 1400 Much stronger in Math
720 680 1400 Stronger reader
700 750 1450 Stretch target

Official facts vs strategy

Everything in this doc is labelled one or the other.

Official (College Board) Not published (do not trust anyone who claims exact numbers)
R&W: 54 questions, 64 minutes, two 32-minute modules The exact Module 1 score needed to get the harder Module 2
Math: 44 questions, 70 minutes, two 35-minute modules How much each question is worth
10-minute break between sections A raw-score-to-scaled-score table for the real test
Module 1 has a mix of easy, medium and hard questions Which questions are unscored trial questions
Module 2 is harder or easier depending on Module 1 performance
No penalty for wrong answers
Desmos graphing calculator is built in for all of Math

How many questions she can miss (estimate)

These ranges come from official practice-test scoring and vary from test to test. Treat them as planning numbers, not rules.

Section score R&W wrong out of 54 Math wrong out of 44
650 about 11 to 13 about 8 to 10
700 about 7 to 9 about 5 to 7
750 about 3 to 5 about 2 to 4

Working budget for 1400: at most 4 wrong per R&W module and at most 3 wrong per Math module.

Why Module 1 matters most (strategy)

Officially, Module 2 difficulty depends on Module 1 performance. The practical consequence: a student routed to the easier Module 2 cannot reach the top of the score range, however well she does there. A 700+ needs the harder Module 2.

  • Treat Module 1 as the accuracy module. Target: at most 2 or 3 wrong.
  • Do not rush Module 1 to bank time. Unused time is worth nothing.
  • Module 1 errors are usually careless ones on easy and medium questions. Those are the cheapest points on the test.
  • If Module 2 feels hard, that is good news. Do not panic. Expect 4 to 6 questions that feel very difficult.

Never sacrifice easy and medium questions

  1. Read the last line of the question first. Know what is being asked before reading anything else.
  2. On Math, write the thing being asked for ("x + y", "the y-intercept", "in minutes") on scratch paper. Check it before clicking.
  3. No question gets more than its time limit on the first pass (see below).
  4. Use the last 3 to 4 minutes of every module to recheck flagged easy questions, not to fight the hardest one.

Time management

Section Per module Average per question First-pass limit
R&W 27 questions, 32 min 71 sec 90 sec, then flag and move
Math 22 questions, 35 min 95 sec 2 min, then flag and move

R&W questions are grouped by type in a fixed order: words in context first, then reading questions, then grammar, then transitions and notes. The last 10 or so (grammar, transitions, notes) are the fastest points. Never run out of time before reaching them.

Math questions run roughly from easier to harder inside each module. Questions 1 to 12 should take about 12 to 14 minutes in total. That leaves 20 minutes for the last 10.

The two-pass system

Pass 1: answer everything that goes smoothly. For anything that stalls, pick the best guess, flag it with Mark for Review, and move on. Never leave a blank.

Pass 2: return to flagged questions in order of how close she was, easiest first.

Skip temporarily when:

  • She has read the question twice and still does not know what it asks.
  • The algebra is on its third line with no end in sight.
  • She is torn between two answers after 75 seconds on R&W.
  • It is a long word problem late in the module and several shorter questions remain.

Guessing

  • Never leave a blank. Wrong and blank score the same.
  • Eliminate first. Two eliminations double the odds.
  • R&W: cross out answers that are too extreme (always, never, proves), off-topic, or true but not asked.
  • Math multiple choice: estimate, or plug the choices into the question, starting with the middle value.
  • Math typed answers: always type something sensible. A negative count or a probability above 1 is never right.
  • With under 60 seconds left, fill every remaining question with the same letter.

Desmos, used strategically

Use Desmos when it is faster than algebra: systems, intersections, roots, vertex, "how many solutions", checking equivalent expressions. Do not use it for one-step arithmetic, simple linear equations, or anything she can do in 15 seconds by hand. Full method in Book 4.

The CBSE student's position

Strong CBSE marks do not convert automatically into a high SAT score. The two exams reward different habits.

CBSE SAT
Math content Calculus, vectors, matrices, 3D geometry Stops at Class 10 level plus functions and basic statistics
What is rewarded Full written method, steps earn marks Only the final answer, fast
Question style Familiar formats from the textbook Simple maths hidden inside unfamiliar wording
Time About 4 to 6 minutes per question About 95 seconds per question
English Long passages, written answers, literature 54 short passages, one question each, one provably correct choice
Grammar Error spotting, formal rules Punctuation and sentence boundaries above all

Where CBSE gives an advantage

  • Algebra manipulation, quadratics, coordinate geometry and trigonometry are well beyond SAT level.
  • Comfort with long calculations and formulas.
  • Formal grammar terms (subject, verb, clause) are already known.

Where CBSE students lose points

  • Over-solving. Writing full solutions when plugging in the choices takes 20 seconds.
  • Word problems in American contexts: miles, feet, gallons, sales tax, tips, discounts.
  • Statistics as interpretation: margin of error, sampling, what a study can conclude. CBSE tests calculation, not meaning.
  • Reading "what does the function model mean" questions. The maths is trivial. The English is the question.
  • Punctuation. Semicolons, colons and dashes are barely tested in CBSE and heavily tested on the SAT.
  • Choosing an answer that is true or sounds sophisticated instead of the one the passage supports.
  • Unfamiliar passage types: 19th-century fiction, poetry, American history, social science studies.
  • Not using the calculator. Many CBSE students never open Desmos.

Diagnostic test (Day 1, October 8)

This 32-question diagnostic maps strengths by domain in 44 minutes. It does not produce a scaled score. The Bluebook test on October 9 does that.

Rules: timer on. No help. Mark each answer with a confidence letter: S (sure), U (unsure), G (guess). Do not look at the key until both parts are done.

Part A: Reading & Writing (16 questions, 19 minutes)

R1. The committee's report was deliberately ______: it listed the costs of each proposal without recommending any of them.

  • A) persuasive
  • B) hasty
  • C) impartial
  • D) obscure

R2. Although early critics dismissed the novelist's spare prose as ______, later readers came to see its plainness as a deliberate and demanding artistic choice.

  • A) ornate
  • B) artless
  • C) derivative
  • D) cryptic

R3. For decades, marine biologists assumed that deep-sea octopuses were solitary. In 2018, however, a submersible off the coast of California filmed thousands of them clustered around warm seafloor vents. Researchers now think the warmth speeds the development of the animals' eggs.

Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence?

  • A) It presents an observation that challenges the assumption described in the first sentence.
  • B) It explains why the assumption in the first sentence was reasonable.
  • C) It offers an example that supports the assumption in the first sentence.
  • D) It questions the methods used by the researchers mentioned in the third sentence.

R4. Text 1: Economist Lena Ortiz argues that remote work raises productivity because employees lose fewer hours to commuting and face fewer interruptions.

Text 2: A study led by Hari Menon tracked 400 software teams. Individual output rose under remote work, but projects that required collaboration across teams took longer to complete.

Based on the texts, how would Menon most likely respond to Ortiz's argument?

  • A) By agreeing that remote work improves every kind of work
  • B) By suggesting that it holds for individual tasks but overlooks collaborative work
  • C) By denying that commuting time affects productivity
  • D) By claiming that interruptions increase under remote work

R5. Urban gardens are often praised as refuges for bees. But ecologist Mara Lind found that city hives of managed honeybees can crowd out wild bee species by competing for the same limited flowers. She suggests that planting more flowers, not adding more hives, is the better way to help pollinators.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

  • A) Managed honeybees collect more pollen than wild bees do.
  • B) Urban gardens provide no benefit to bees.
  • C) Lind believes that cities should ban beekeeping.
  • D) Adding honeybee hives to cities may harm wild bees, so increasing flowers is a better approach.

R6. A historian claims that the printing press spread slowly in one region mainly because few people there could read, not because presses were expensive.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's claim?

  • A) Presses cost less in the region than elsewhere, yet almost none were bought in towns with few readers.
  • B) Presses were expensive in every region during the period.
  • C) Literacy in the region rose sharply after presses arrived.
  • D) The region's rulers banned several books during the period.

R7. Mean plant height after four weeks

Daily light (hours) Soil A (cm) Soil B (cm)
6 12 11
10 19 14
14 27 15

Students concluded that additional light increased growth far more in soil A than in soil B. Which choice best uses data from the table to support this conclusion?

  • A) At 6 hours of light, plants in soil A were 1 cm taller than plants in soil B.
  • B) At 14 hours of light, plants in soil A reached 27 cm.
  • C) From 6 to 14 hours of light, height rose by 15 cm in soil A but by only 4 cm in soil B.
  • D) From 6 to 10 hours of light, height in soil B rose by 3 cm.

R8. Birds that migrate at night typically call more often in fog. Researchers recording over a brightly lit city found call rates on clear nights as high as those normally recorded in fog. Since calling is thought to help disoriented birds stay together, this finding suggests that ______

  • A) fog is more common over cities than over rural areas.
  • B) artificial light may disorient migrating birds much as fog does.
  • C) migrating birds prefer to fly over cities.
  • D) frequent calling causes birds to become disoriented.

R9. The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has mapped the Moon's surface since ______ images reveal features as small as a meter across.

  • A) 2009, its
  • B) 2009 its
  • C) 2009; its
  • D) 2009, and, its

R10. The collection of letters written by the two scientists over three decades ______ now housed in the university archive.

  • A) are
  • B) is
  • C) were
  • D) have been

R11. The chemist Asima ______ developed drugs to treat epilepsy and malaria.

  • A) Chatterjee who studied plant compounds,
  • B) Chatterjee, who studied plant compounds,
  • C) Chatterjee, who studied plant compounds
  • D) Chatterjee who studied plant compounds

R12. Having tested the bridge design in a wind tunnel, ______

  • A) the engineers approved the plan for construction.
  • B) the plan was approved by the engineers for construction.
  • C) construction was approved by the engineers.
  • D) approval for construction was given by the engineers.

R13. The city expected the new bike lanes to reduce car traffic. ______ traffic counts a year later were virtually unchanged.

  • A) Accordingly,
  • B) However,
  • C) In addition,
  • D) For instance,

R14. Glaciers in the range lost mass in every year of the study. ______ the smallest glaciers, which had the least ice to begin with, disappeared entirely.

  • A) Nevertheless,
  • B) By contrast,
  • C) Likewise,
  • D) In fact,

R15. A student has taken these notes:

  • The baobab tree stores water in its trunk.
  • A single trunk can hold up to 120,000 liters.
  • The trunk swells in the rainy season and shrinks in the dry season.
  • Elephants strip baobab bark for moisture during droughts.

The student wants to emphasize how much water a baobab can store. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

  • A) A single baobab trunk can hold up to 120,000 liters of water.
  • B) The baobab's trunk swells in the rainy season and shrinks in the dry season.
  • C) During droughts, elephants strip baobab bark for moisture.
  • D) The baobab stores water in its trunk, a fact elephants take advantage of.

R16. A student has taken these notes:

  • In 2021, linguist Dana Reyes studied text messages from 300 teenagers.
  • She wanted to know whether texting abbreviations weaken formal writing.
  • She compared each participant's texts with their school essays.
  • Heavy users of abbreviations scored no lower on essays than other participants.

The student wants to present the study's finding. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

  • A) In 2021, Dana Reyes studied text messages from 300 teenagers.
  • B) Reyes wanted to know whether texting abbreviations weaken formal writing.
  • C) Reyes found that teenagers who used many abbreviations wrote essays as well as other teenagers did.
  • D) Reyes compared teenagers' text messages with their school essays.

Part B: Math (16 questions, 25 minutes, Desmos allowed)

M1. If 3(x - 4) = 2x + 5, what is the value of x?

M2. A line passes through (2, 5) and (6, 13). What is its y-intercept?

  • A) -1
  • B) 1
  • C) 2
  • D) 5

M3. 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 1. What is the value of x + y?

M4. Plan A costs $30 a month plus $0.10 per minute. Plan B costs $0.25 per minute with no monthly fee. For which monthly usage is Plan A cheaper?

  • A) Fewer than 120 minutes
  • B) More than 120 minutes
  • C) Fewer than 200 minutes
  • D) More than 200 minutes

M5. The system 3x - 2y = 8 and 6x + ky = 10 has no solution. What is the value of k?

M6. What is the positive solution of x2 - 5x - 14 = 0?

M7. What is the minimum value of f(x) = x2 - 6x - 7?

  • A) -7
  • B) -9
  • C) -16
  • D) 3

M8. Which expression is equivalent to (x3 y2)2 / (x2 y), where x and y are not zero?

  • A) x4 y3
  • B) x3 y3
  • C) x8 y3
  • D) x4 y4

M9. A culture of 500 bacteria doubles every 3 hours. Which function gives the number of bacteria after t hours?

  • A) 500(2)3t
  • B) 500(2)t/3
  • C) 500(3)t/2
  • D) 500 + 2t/3

M10. What are all the solutions of sqrt(x + 6) = x?

  • A) -2 only
  • B) 3 only
  • C) -2 and 3
  • D) There is no solution.

M11. A price is increased by 20% and the new price is then decreased by 20%. What is the net change from the original price?

  • A) No change
  • B) 4% increase
  • C) 2% decrease
  • D) 4% decrease

M12. The mean of five numbers is 12. When a sixth number is added, the mean becomes 13. What is the sixth number?

M13. In a random sample of 200 students at a school, 62% prefer a later start time. The margin of error is 5%. Which conclusion is best supported?

  • A) It is plausible that between 57% and 67% of all students at the school prefer a later start time.
  • B) Exactly 62% of all students at the school prefer a later start time.
  • C) About 62% of all students in the country prefer a later start time.
  • D) About 5% of the sampled students answered incorrectly.

M14. A right triangle has legs of length 9 and 12. What is the sine of the angle opposite the side of length 9?

  • A) 3/4
  • B) 4/5
  • C) 3/5
  • D) 5/3

M15. A circle has equation x2 + y2 - 4x + 10y = 20. What is its radius?

M16. Triangles ABC and DEF are similar, with AB corresponding to DE. AB = 6, DE = 9, and the area of triangle ABC is 20. What is the area of triangle DEF?

Diagnostic answer key (cover until both parts are done)

Q Answer Domain Skill Why
R1 C Craft and Structure Words in context Listing costs without recommending means neutral.
R2 B Craft and Structure Words in context "Dismissed" plus "plainness" means critics thought it unskilled. "Although" signals later readers disagreed.
R3 A Craft and Structure Function "However" introduces evidence against the old assumption.
R4 B Craft and Structure Paired texts Menon confirms part and limits part.
R5 D Information and Ideas Main idea Covers both the problem and Lind's suggestion. C is too extreme.
R6 A Information and Ideas Textual evidence Cheap presses still unsold where few read: cost ruled out, literacy isolated. C reverses cause and effect.
R7 C Information and Ideas Data evidence Only C compares the change in both soils.
R8 B Information and Ideas Inference Same behaviour as in fog, so the same likely cause: disorientation.
R9 C Conventions Sentence boundaries Two complete sentences. Comma alone is a comma splice.
R10 B Conventions Subject-verb agreement Subject is "collection", singular.
R11 B Conventions Nonessential clause Extra information needs a comma on both sides.
R12 A Conventions Modifier The engineers did the testing, so they must follow the comma.
R13 B Expression of Ideas Transition Expectation, then the opposite result.
R14 D Expression of Ideas Transition Second sentence intensifies the first.
R15 A Expression of Ideas Notes Only A gives the amount.
R16 C Expression of Ideas Notes Only C states the result.

Reading the results

Domain score Meaning Action in the plan
4 of 4 (or 5 of 5) Strong Timed practice at Level 3 and 4 only
3 Leak One concept review, then Level 2 and 3
2 or fewer Priority gap Add 20 minutes a day on this domain in week 1

Also check: any question marked S (sure) but wrong is the most dangerous kind. Log it first. If either part ran past its time limit, timing is a weakness in its own right.

Error classification

Code Type Typical fix
A Did not know the concept Learn the rule or formula, then do 5 questions on it
B Knew the concept, applied it wrongly Redo the question unaided, write the correct steps
C Careless mistake Add a specific check (for example "circle what is asked")
D Misread the question Read the last line first, underline the quantity asked
E Time pressure Apply the skip rule earlier, drill that question type timed
F Guessing Find out which of A to E was underneath the guess
G Calculation error Use Desmos for arithmetic, write one step per line

How to record a mistake

  1. Log it the same day, before looking at the explanation.
  2. Try the question again untimed. If she gets it right now, the code is C, D, E or G. If not, it is A or B.
  3. Write one sentence in her own words: "I got this wrong because...". "Silly mistake" is not allowed. Name the exact slip.
  4. Write the clue she should have noticed.
  5. Set a retry date 3 days later. A question leaves the log only after two correct retries.
  6. Count codes every Friday. The most frequent code decides the next week's focus.

Book 2

Reading & Writing Mastery

How the section is built

Every R&W question has its own short passage (25 to 150 words) and exactly one answer that the text proves. The four domains appear in this approximate mix.

Domain Share Questions of 54 Speed of improvement
Craft and Structure about 28% 13 to 15 Medium
Information and Ideas about 26% 12 to 14 Slow to medium
Standard English Conventions about 26% 11 to 15 Fast
Expression of Ideas about 20% 8 to 12 Fast

The universal reading method

  1. Question first. Read the question stem before the passage. It tells her what job the passage is doing.
  2. One careful read. Read once, at normal speed, hunting only for what the question asked. No rereading the whole passage. If needed, reread one sentence.
  3. Predict. Say the answer in her own words before looking at the choices.
  4. Eliminate. Cross out three wrong answers. Do not hunt for the right one.
  5. Prove. Point to the exact words that support the choice. No proof, no click.

The five wrong-answer types

Type What it looks like Quick test
Too strong always, never, all, proves, completely Does the passage say "some" or "may"?
Out of scope Sensible, but never mentioned Can she point to it in the text?
Half right First half matches, second half does not Read every word of the choice
Reversed Right topic, opposite relationship Check who did what to whom
True but irrelevant In the passage, but does not answer this question Reread the question stem

Information and Ideas

Main idea and details

Concept. The main idea is what the whole passage says, not one detail from it.

How the SAT tests it. "Which choice best states the main idea?" or "According to the text, why did X happen?"

30-second method. Read the first and last sentences with extra care. Summarise in 8 words. Pick the choice that matches the summary and covers the whole text.

Traps. A detail from one sentence offered as the main idea. A choice that goes beyond the text. In fiction, a choice that names an emotion the passage never shows.

When stuck. Ask of each choice: "Is this about the whole passage or one line?" Drop the one-liners.

Inference

Concept. The answer is the smallest logical step from what is stated. It is never a creative leap.

How the SAT tests it. A passage ending in a blank: "...this suggests that ______".

30-second method. Find the two facts the passage sets side by side. The answer connects them and adds nothing new.

Traps. A reasonable real-world belief that the passage does not support. An answer that explains too much.

When stuck. Choose the most boring, most cautious choice that uses the passage's own terms.

Textual evidence

Concept. A claim is given. She picks the finding or quotation that would support (or weaken) it.

30-second method. Underline the claim. Split it into parts: who, what effect, compared with what. The right answer matches every part.

Traps. Same topic, different claim. Correlation offered where the claim is about cause. Evidence for the opposite direction.

When stuck. Ask: "If this choice were true, would a sceptic have to accept the claim?"

Data evidence (tables and graphs)

Concept. The same task, with numbers. The data are simple. The question is which numbers match the claim.

30-second method. Read the claim first. Go to the table only for the rows the claim names. A claim about change needs two data points. A claim about comparison needs two groups.

Traps. A choice that reads the table correctly but does not support the claim. This is the most common wrong answer.

When stuck. Eliminate any choice that mentions only one of the two things being compared.

Craft and Structure

Words in context

Concept. Pick the word that fits the precise meaning the sentence needs. The sentence always contains a clue.

30-second method. Cover the choices. Find the clue (often after a colon, or signalled by although, but, because). Put her own simple word in the blank. Match it.

Traps. A word that sounds academic but has the wrong meaning. A word with the right meaning but wrong charge (positive vs negative). A common word used in its second meaning.

When stuck. Decide positive or negative first. That usually removes two choices. Never pick a word only because it is unfamiliar.

High-frequency words to know

Group Words
Support bolster, corroborate, substantiate, underscore, validate
Weaken or oppose undermine, refute, contradict, dispute, counter
Uncertain tentative, ambiguous, equivocal, speculative, inconclusive
Careful or neutral meticulous, impartial, prudent, pragmatic, empirical
Change alter, supplant, diverge, fluctuate, mitigate, exacerbate
New or unusual novel, unprecedented, anomalous, innovative, idiosyncratic
Common or ordinary ubiquitous, prevalent, conventional, mundane, prosaic
Tone wry, candid, ambivalent, indifferent, reverent, dismissive

Add every unknown word from practice to a personal list with the sentence it appeared in. Ten a day.

Text structure and purpose

Concept. What a sentence or passage does, not what it says.

How the SAT tests it. "Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?" or "...the overall structure of the text?"

30-second method. Label the sentence with a verb: introduces, concedes, contrasts, explains, gives an example, qualifies. Match the verb first, then the content.

Traps. A choice with the right content and the wrong verb. For example "criticises" when the text only "describes".

When stuck. Look at the first word of the next sentence. "However", "for example" and "therefore" reveal the role of what came before.

Paired texts

Concept. Two short texts on one topic. The question asks how one author would respond to the other.

30-second method. Write one line for each: "Text 1 says X." "Text 2 says Y." Then name the relationship: agrees, disagrees, agrees in part, adds a limit.

Traps. Total agreement or total rejection when Text 2 only qualifies Text 1. The qualified answer is right far more often.

When stuck. Eliminate anything that puts words in an author's mouth that are not in their text.

Poetry and older fiction

Read for the literal situation first: who is speaking, to whom, about what. Translate each long sentence into plain English. The question is still a main idea or function question.

Reading practice

No answers here. The key is at the end of this book.

P1 (medium, main idea). Meera had rehearsed her apology on the train, shaping each sentence until it sounded sincere. But when her grandmother opened the door and simply held out a cup of tea, the sentences dissolved, and Meera found she could only say, "I'm late."

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

  • A) Meera resents having to apologise to her grandmother.
  • B) Meera's prepared words desert her when she is met with unexpected kindness.
  • C) Meera's grandmother is angry about her lateness.
  • D) Meera dislikes travelling by train.

P2 (hard, inference). Economists studying a coastal town found that after a new highway cut travel time to the nearest city in half, the number of shops in the town fell, even though residents' incomes rose. Residents, it seems, ______

  • A) began doing more of their shopping in the city.
  • B) spent less money overall than before.
  • C) moved to the city in large numbers.
  • D) had opposed the building of the highway.

P3 (hard, evidence). Biologist Ines Okafor hypothesises that a desert beetle collects water from fog by means of the bumpy texture of its back rather than its body's chemical coating.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?

  • A) The beetles collect most of their water at dawn.
  • B) Beetles from foggier regions tend to have more bumps.
  • C) Beetles with the coating removed collected as much water as untreated beetles, while beetles with smoothed backs collected almost none.
  • D) The chemical coating repels water in laboratory tests.

P4 (medium, data).

Year Library visits (thousands) E-book loans (thousands)
2019 410 95
2021 260 240
2023 395 250

A librarian argues that the growth in e-book loans did not come at the lasting expense of in-person visits. Which choice best supports this argument?

  • A) E-book loans rose from 95 thousand to 240 thousand between 2019 and 2021.
  • B) Visits fell by 150 thousand between 2019 and 2021.
  • C) In 2021, visits exceeded e-book loans.
  • D) By 2023, visits had nearly returned to their 2019 level while e-book loans remained far above theirs.

P5 (medium, words in context). The architect's design was praised for its ______ use of space: every corridor doubled as storage, and no room served only one purpose.

  • A) lavish
  • B) economical
  • C) conventional
  • D) haphazard

P6 (hard, words in context). The critic noted that the film's final scene ______ the ambiguity of its opening: what had seemed a mystery is revealed as a simple misunderstanding.

  • A) compounds
  • B) echoes
  • C) resolves
  • D) anticipates

P7 (hard, function). Many textbooks describe the heart as a simple pump. The comparison is useful up to a point. A pump, however, does not adjust its own rhythm, repair its own valves, or respond to the chemistry of the fluid it moves.

Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence?

  • A) It concedes the value of the comparison while signalling that its limits will follow.
  • B) It rejects the comparison made in the first sentence.
  • C) It explains how a mechanical pump works.
  • D) It gives an example of a textbook that uses the comparison.

P8 (hard, paired texts). Text 1: Archaeologists have long held that farming spread across Europe as farmers migrated and replaced hunter-gatherers.

Text 2: Geneticist Paulo Reis analysed ancient DNA from one river valley. He found that early farmers there descended largely from local hunter-gatherers, suggesting that the practice, not the people, had moved in.

How would Reis most likely characterise the view in Text 1?

  • A) As fully consistent with his findings
  • B) As disproved for the whole of Europe
  • C) As based mainly on genetic evidence
  • D) As failing to hold in at least one region

Standard English Conventions

This is the fastest domain to fix. About 12 rules cover nearly every question. The answer is decided by a rule, never by what "sounds right".

30-second method for every grammar question

  1. Look at the choices before reading the passage. See what changes between them.
  2. If punctuation changes, it is a boundary question. Check whether the words on each side form a complete sentence.
  3. If the verb changes, find the subject and the time markers.
  4. If a pronoun or apostrophe changes, find the noun it refers to.
  5. Apply the rule. Do not reread the passage for meaning.

Sentence boundaries (the most tested rule)

A complete sentence has a subject, a main verb and a complete thought. Two complete sentences can be joined in only these ways.

Join Example Legal?
Period The lab closed. The team moved. Yes
Semicolon The lab closed; the team moved. Yes
Comma + and, but, so, or, yet, for, nor The lab closed, so the team moved. Yes
Colon or single dash The lab closed: funding had run out. Yes, if the first part is complete
Comma alone The lab closed, the team moved. No. Comma splice.
Nothing The lab closed the team moved. No. Run-on.

Shortcuts

  • A semicolon equals a period. If a period would not work, a semicolon will not either.
  • If two choices differ only in period vs semicolon, both are wrong.
  • However, therefore, moreover, thus and for example are not joining words. Between two sentences write "; however," or ". However,".
  • Words like because, although, while, which and who make a clause incomplete. An incomplete clause joins with a comma or nothing, never a semicolon.

Trap. A long sentence with a descriptive phrase in the middle hides where the first sentence ends. Find the two main verbs.

Colons and dashes

  • A colon must come after a complete sentence. It introduces a list, an explanation or an example.
  • Never put a colon after "such as", "including" or a verb ("The colours are: red..." is wrong).
  • One dash works like a colon. Two dashes work like two commas around extra information.
  • Punctuation must match: comma with comma, dash with dash. Never one of each.

Commas

Use a comma Do not use a comma
Around extra (removable) information, on both sides Between a subject and its verb
After an introductory phrase Before "that"
Between items in a list of three or more Between a verb and its object
Before and, but, so when joining two full sentences Around information the sentence needs

Names and titles. "The physicist Lise Meitner discovered..." takes no commas, because the name is needed to know which physicist. "Lise Meitner, a physicist, discovered..." takes two, because the description is extra.

Removal test. Delete the words between the commas. If the sentence still works and still identifies its subject, the commas are right.

Apostrophes and possessives

Form Meaning Example
scientist's belonging to one scientist the scientist's notes
scientists' belonging to several the scientists' notes
scientists plural, no ownership the scientists met
its / it's belonging to it / it is its orbit, it's late
their / they're / there belonging to them / they are / place their data
whose / who's belonging to whom / who is whose idea

Method. Ask two questions: one owner or many? Is anything owned at all? A noun followed directly by another noun usually owns it.

Subject-verb agreement

  • Find the true subject. Cross out everything between "of", "in", "with" and the verb. "The box of letters is here."
  • Each, every, either, neither, anyone and everyone are singular.
  • In inverted sentences the subject comes after the verb. "Among the ruins were two statues."
  • Two subjects joined by "and" are plural.

Trap. A plural noun placed right before the verb when the real subject is singular and far away.

Pronouns

  • A pronoun matches its noun in number. A company is "it", not "they". Researchers are "they".
  • The reference must be clear. If "it" could mean two things, the right answer names the noun.

Verb tense and verb form

  • Match the time markers ("in 1920", "since 2010", "currently") and the other verbs nearby.
  • "Since" and "for the past" need has or have + verb. A finished past date needs simple past.
  • Every sentence needs a real main verb. "The author, writing in 1850, argues..." is complete. "The author, writing in 1850, arguing..." is not.
  • Words ending in -ing, or starting with "to", cannot be the main verb alone.

Modifiers

An opening descriptive phrase must be followed immediately by the thing it describes. "Walking to school, Riya saw the rainbow." Not "Walking to school, the rainbow was seen by Riya."

Method. Ask "who or what is doing this?" That noun must come right after the comma.

Parallelism

Items in a list or comparison take the same form. "She likes reading, writing and painting." "To plan is easier than to act."

Concision and redundancy

The Digital SAT rarely tests this directly. One rule still helps: when two choices are both grammatically correct and mean the same, the shorter one is right. Never repeat an idea already stated ("annually each year").

Expression of Ideas

Transitions

Concept. Choose the word that names the logical link between two sentences.

30-second method. Cover the choices. Read the sentence before and the sentence after. Decide the relationship: same direction, opposite direction, cause and effect, example, or sequence. Then pick from that group.

Relationship Transitions
Addition moreover, furthermore, in addition, also
Contrast however, nevertheless, by contrast, on the other hand, still
Cause and effect therefore, consequently, as a result, thus, accordingly
Example for example, for instance, specifically
Emphasis in fact, indeed
Restatement in other words, that is
Similarity similarly, likewise
Sequence first, next, subsequently, finally, meanwhile
Alternative instead, alternatively, rather

Shortcuts and traps

  • If two choices mean the same ("therefore" and "consequently"), both are wrong.
  • "In fact" strengthens the previous point. It does not contrast.
  • "Nevertheless" means "despite that". "By contrast" compares two different things. They are not interchangeable.
  • "Similarly" needs two different subjects doing alike things.

When stuck. Test "but", "so" and "and" in the gap. Whichever fits tells her the group.

Notes questions

Concept. Bullet-point notes, then a goal. Only one choice does what the goal says.

30-second method. Skip the notes. Read the goal and underline its key words ("emphasise a difference", "introduce the study to a new audience", "present the finding"). Check each choice against the goal only.

Traps. Every choice is true and well written. The wrong ones just do a different job. A "difference" needs two things. A "similarity" needs "both". A "new audience" needs a brief explanation of who or what.

When stuck. If the goal has two parts, eliminate any choice that covers only one.

Writing practice

G1 (easy). The museum's new wing opens next ______ will display over 300 textiles.

  • A) month, it
  • B) month it
  • C) month; it
  • D) month: and it

G2 (medium). Researchers identified three factors behind the ______ habitat loss, pollution, and invasive species.

  • A) decline;
  • B) decline:
  • C) decline, being
  • D) decline.

G3 (medium). The drug performed well in early ______ later studies revealed serious side effects.

  • A) trials, however,
  • B) trials however,
  • C) trials, however;
  • D) trials; however,

G4 (medium). Each of the paintings in the two galleries ______ been restored within the last decade.

  • A) has
  • B) have
  • C) were
  • D) are

G5 (hard). Among the artifacts recovered from the shipwreck ______ a bronze astrolabe and several glass beads.

  • A) was
  • B) is
  • C) were
  • D) has been

G6 (medium). The two ______ findings appeared in the same journal, but ______ conclusions differed.

  • A) team's ... there
  • B) teams ... they're
  • C) teams' ... they're
  • D) teams' ... their

G7 (hard). The poet Joy Harjo, whose work often draws on Muscogee history, ______ as US poet laureate from 2019 to 2022.

  • A) serving
  • B) served
  • C) having served
  • D) to serve

G8 (medium). Known for its bright orange wings, ______

  • A) scientists track the monarch butterfly across North America.
  • B) the monarch butterfly is tracked by scientists across North America.
  • C) North America is where scientists track the monarch butterfly.
  • D) tracking of the monarch butterfly is done across North America.

G9 (medium). The internship taught her to analyse data, to write reports, and ______

  • A) presenting findings.
  • B) she presented findings.
  • C) to present findings.
  • D) the presentation of findings.

G10 (hard). The ______ designed the footbridge in 1998.

  • A) engineer Ravi Nair
  • B) engineer, Ravi Nair,
  • C) engineer, Ravi Nair
  • D) engineer Ravi Nair,

G11 (hard). The ______ a relative of the giraffe native to central Africa—was unknown to Western science until 1901.

  • A) okapi,
  • B) okapi;
  • C) okapi
  • D) okapi—

G12 (medium). When a company cuts prices, ______ often hopes to attract new customers.

  • A) it
  • B) they
  • C) one
  • D) those

T1 (medium). The team's first prototype overheated within minutes. ______ the second, which used a ceramic casing, ran for six hours without trouble.

  • A) Similarly,
  • B) As a result,
  • C) By contrast,
  • D) In other words,

T2 (medium). Sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze on kelp. ______ where otters disappear, urchin numbers surge and kelp forests shrink.

  • A) Nevertheless,
  • B) For instance,
  • C) Alternatively,
  • D) Consequently,

T3 (hard). Critics called the proposal unrealistic. The mayor, ______ pressed ahead with it.

  • A) therefore,
  • B) nevertheless,
  • C) for example,
  • D) likewise,

Answer key for this book

Q Answer Reason
P1 B The apology "dissolved" when she was offered tea. Nothing shows anger or resentment.
P2 A Incomes up, local shops down, city now close. The smallest step is that spending moved to the city.
P3 C Tests both factors separately. B is only a correlation. D is about the coating, not the bumps.
P4 D "Lasting" needs the 2023 recovery. A, B and C read the table correctly but do not support the claim.
P5 B The clue after the colon: nothing wasted.
P6 C The mystery is explained, so the ambiguity ends. "Compounds" means makes worse.
P7 A "Useful up to a point" grants value and warns of limits. "However" follows.
P8 D One valley only. B is too strong.
G1 C Two complete sentences.
G2 B Complete sentence, then a list.
G3 D "However" between two sentences takes a semicolon before and a comma after.
G4 A Subject is "each", singular.
G5 C Inverted. Subject is "an astrolabe and several beads", plural.
G6 D Two teams own the findings. "Their" shows ownership.
G7 B The sentence needs a main verb in the past.
G8 B The butterfly has the orange wings.
G9 C Matches "to analyse" and "to write".
G10 A The name is essential. No commas, and none between subject and verb.
G11 D The closing dash needs an opening dash.
G12 A "Company" is singular.
T1 C Two prototypes, opposite results.
T2 D Cause and effect.
T3 B He went ahead despite the criticism.

Book 3

Math Mastery

How the section is built

Algebra and Advanced Math make up about 70% of the Math section. They get most of the study time.

Domain Share Questions of 44 Priority
Algebra about 35% 13 to 15 1
Advanced Math about 35% 13 to 15 1
Problem-Solving and Data Analysis about 15% 5 to 7 2
Geometry and Trigonometry about 15% 5 to 7 2

About three quarters of questions are multiple choice. The rest need a typed answer. A reference sheet with basic geometry formulas is available on screen.

The four-step routine for every Math question

  1. Read the last sentence first. Write down what is asked ("2x", "y-intercept", "in hours").
  2. Choose the route: by hand, Desmos, or plug in the choices. Decide in 5 seconds.
  3. Solve, one step per line.
  4. Before clicking, look back at what she wrote in step 1. Answer that, not x.

Three non-algebra weapons

  • Plug in the choices. When the choices are numbers and the question asks "what is x", test the middle choice first.
  • Pick numbers. When the question has variables in the choices or percentages with no starting amount, choose easy numbers (100 for percentages, 2 or 3 for variables). Avoid 0 and 1.
  • Desmos. See Book 4.

Algebra

Linear equations

Concept. Do the same thing to both sides until x is alone.

Number of solutions. Simplify to ax + b = cx + d.

Condition Solutions
a and c differ Exactly one
a = c, b and d differ None
a = c and b = d Infinitely many

Traps. Forgetting to distribute a negative sign. Solving for x when 3x + 1 was asked.

Desmos. Type each side as its own line and find the intersection. Do not use it for two-step equations. By hand is faster.

Linear functions

Form Equation Reads off directly
Slope-intercept y = mx + b Slope m, y-intercept b
Standard Ax + By = C Slope -A/B, x-intercept C/A, y-intercept C/B
Point-slope y - y1 = m(x - x1) A point and the slope
  • Slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
  • Parallel lines: equal slopes. Perpendicular lines: slopes multiply to -1.
  • In a word problem, the slope is the rate ("per hour") and the y-intercept is the starting amount.

Traps. Swapping x and y in the slope formula. Reading the intercept as the rate in an interpretation question.

Systems of equations

Methods. Substitution when one variable is already alone. Elimination when coefficients line up.

Shortcut. If the question asks for x + y or 3x - y, try adding or subtracting the two equations first. The answer often appears without solving for either variable.

No solution or infinitely many. Write both in the form Ax + By = C. Same ratio of A and B but different C means no solution. All three in the same ratio means infinitely many.

Desmos. Type both equations exactly as given and click the intersection. This is almost always the fastest route for a system with awkward numbers.

When not to use Desmos. When the system contains an unknown constant like k. Use the ratio rule.

Inequalities

  • Multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the sign.
  • "At least" means >=. "At most" and "no more than" mean <=. "More than" means >.
  • For a system of inequalities, Desmos shades each region. A point is a solution only if it lies in the overlap.

Absolute value

  • If the absolute value of (x - a) equals b, then x = a + b or x = a - b.
  • An absolute value can never equal a negative number. That equation has no solution.
  • "Less than b" gives a band between the two values. "Greater than b" gives the two outside regions.

Word problems

Method. Name the variables with letters that mean something (a for adults, s for students). Write one equation for the count and one for the money. Check that the answer is the variable asked for.

Traps. Units (minutes vs hours). A one-time fee treated as a rate. Answering with the wrong variable.

Algebra practice

A1 (easy). 5x - 7 = 2x + 14. What is x?

A2 (easy). A line has slope -3 and passes through (2, 4). What is its y-intercept?

A3 (medium). 3x + 2y = 16 and x + 2y = 8. What is x - y?

A4 (medium). A taxi charges $3.50 plus $1.25 per kilometre. A ride cost $16.00. How many kilometres was it?

A5 (medium). What is the sum of the solutions of the equation: the absolute value of (2x - 5) equals 9?

A6 (hard). The equation 4(x - 2) + c = 4x + 1 has infinitely many solutions. What is c?

A7 (hard). Line k is perpendicular to 2x + 5y = 10 and passes through (4, 1). What is the y-intercept of line k?

A8 (hard). Adult tickets cost $12 and student tickets cost $8. A total of 150 tickets were sold for $1,480. How many student tickets were sold?

Advanced Math

Quadratics

Form Equation Shows
Standard y = ax2 + bx + c y-intercept c
Factored y = a(x - r)(x - s) x-intercepts r and s
Vertex y = a(x - h)2 + k Vertex (h, k)
Fact Formula
Vertex x-coordinate x = -b / (2a)
Sum of solutions -b / a
Product of solutions c / a
Discriminant b2 - 4ac
Quadratic formula x = (-b plus or minus sqrt(b2 - 4ac)) / (2a)
Discriminant Real solutions Graph
Positive Two Crosses the x-axis twice
Zero One Touches the x-axis
Negative None Does not meet the x-axis

Shortcuts. The vertex lies halfway between the two x-intercepts. If a is positive the vertex is a minimum. If a is negative it is a maximum. "Which form shows the minimum as a constant?" always means vertex form.

Traps. In vertex form y = (x - 3)2 + 5 the vertex is at x = 3, not -3. Forgetting the second solution. Dividing both sides by x and losing x = 0.

Desmos. Graph it. Click the x-intercepts for roots and the turning point for the vertex.

When not to use Desmos. When the quadratic has an unknown constant and the question asks for the value that gives one solution. Use the discriminant, or use a slider (Book 4).

Factoring patterns

  • a2 - b2 = (a + b)(a - b)
  • a2 + 2ab + b2 = (a + b)2
  • a2 - 2ab + b2 = (a - b)2
  • For x2 + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

Exponents and radicals

Rule Example
xa times xb = xa + b x2 times x5 = x7
xa / xb = xa - b x7 / x2 = x5
(xa)b = xab (x2)3 = x6
x-a = 1 / xa 2-3 = 1/8
x0 = 1 50 = 1
xa/b = the b-th root of xa 82/3 = 4

Traps. (x + y)2 is not x2 + y2. Squaring both sides of a radical equation can create a false solution. Always check answers in the original equation.

Polynomials

  • If p(a) = 0, then (x - a) is a factor and a is an x-intercept.
  • The remainder when p(x) is divided by (x - a) equals p(a).
  • The number of distinct x-intercepts is the number of distinct real zeros.

Rational expressions

  • To add fractions, use a common denominator. To solve an equation with fractions, multiply every term by the common denominator.
  • Any value that makes a denominator zero is excluded. Check the final answer against it.

Nonlinear systems

Set the two expressions for y equal and solve the resulting quadratic. Its discriminant gives the number of intersection points. In Desmos, graph both and count or click the intersections.

Functions

  • f(3) means replace x with 3.
  • f(g(x)) means work from the inside out.
  • f(x) + k moves the graph up k. f(x - h) moves it right h. -f(x) flips it over the x-axis.
  • From a table or graph: f(2) = 5 means the point (2, 5).

Exponential functions

Model Meaning
y = a(b)x a is the starting value, b is the factor per step
b = 1 + r Growth at rate r (5% growth gives 1.05)
b = 1 - r Decay at rate r (8% decay gives 0.92)
y = a(2)t/k Doubles every k units of time

Linear or exponential? Equal differences each step mean linear. Equal ratios (or equal percentages) each step mean exponential.

Traps. Reading 0.92 as a 92% decrease. Using 3t instead of t/3 for "every 3 hours".

Advanced Math practice

Q1 (easy). What are the solutions of x2 - 9x + 20 = 0?

Q2 (easy). If 2x + 1 = 32, what is x?

Q3 (medium). f(x) = 2(x - 3)2 + 5. What is the vertex of the graph of y = f(x) + 2?

Q4 (medium). What is the sum of the solutions of 2x2 - 12x + 7 = 0?

Q5 (medium). If x3/2 = 27, what is x?

Q6 (medium). $2,000 is invested at 5% annual growth, compounded yearly. What is it worth after 2 years?

Q7 (hard). For what value of c does x2 - 8x + c = 0 have exactly one real solution?

Q8 (hard). The line y = 2x + k touches the parabola y = x2 - 4x + 5 at exactly one point. What is k?

Q9 (hard). p(x) = x3 - 2x2 + kx - 6, and (x - 3) is a factor of p(x). What is k?

Q10 (hard). What is the positive solution of 1/(x - 1) + 1/(x + 1) = 3/4?

Q11 (hard). P(t) = 1200(0.92)t models a town's population t years after 2020. Which is the best interpretation of 0.92?

  • A) The population decreases by 92% each year.
  • B) The population decreases by 8% each year.
  • C) The population decreases by 0.92 people each year.
  • D) The population in 2020 was 0.92 thousand.

Q1 4 and 5 (x - 4)(x - 5) Click the x-intercepts
Q2 4 32 = 25 Not needed
Q3 (3, 7) Vertex (3, 5) moved up 2 Graph and click the minimum
Q4 6 -b/a = 12/2 Add the two x-intercepts
Q5 9 x = 272/3 = 32 Type 272/3
Q6 $2,205 2000(1.05)2 Type it
Q7 16 64 - 4c = 0 Slider on c until the graph touches the axis
Q8 -4 x2 - 6x + 5 - k = 0, so 36 - 4(5 - k) = 0 Slider on k until line and parabola touch
Q9 -1 p(3) = 27 - 18 + 3k - 6 = 0 Not suited
Q10 3 2x/(x2 - 1) = 3/4 gives 3x2 - 8x - 3 = 0 Graph both sides, click the intersection
Q11 B 0.92 = 1 - 0.08 Not suited

Problem-Solving and Data Analysis

The arithmetic here is easy. The reading is where points are lost. This is the domain where CBSE students most need to adjust.

Ratios, rates and units

  • Write a proportion with the same units in the same positions: km/h = km/h.
  • For unit conversion, multiply by fractions equal to 1 and cancel units. 54 km/h = 54 x 1000 m / 3600 s = 15 m/s.
  • Distance = rate x time. Work done = rate x time. Density = mass / volume.

Traps. A ratio of 3:5 means 3 parts of 8, not 3 parts of 5. Squared units convert by the square of the factor (1 m2 = 10,000 cm2).

Percentages

Task Method
p% of n (p/100) x n
Increase by p% Multiply by (1 + p/100)
Decrease by p% Multiply by (1 - p/100)
Percent change (new - old) / old x 100
Find the original after a change Divide by the multiplier
Two changes in a row Multiply the two multipliers

Traps. A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall is not zero change. "Percent of" and "percent greater than" differ: 150 is 150% of 100 but 50% greater than 100.

Shortcut. If no starting value is given, use 100.

Statistics

Measure Meaning Effect of one extreme value
Mean Sum divided by count Pulled strongly toward it
Median Middle value when sorted Barely moves
Range Largest minus smallest Increases
Standard deviation How spread out the values are Increases
  • Total = mean x count. Most mean questions are solved with this.
  • The SAT never asks for a standard deviation calculation. It asks which data set is more spread out.
  • From a frequency table or dot plot, find the median by counting to the middle position.

Probability and two-way tables

Probability = favourable outcomes / total outcomes. In a two-way table, the words after "given that" or "of the students who" tell her which row or column is the new total.

Scatterplots and lines of best fit

  • The slope of the line of best fit is the predicted change in y for each 1-unit increase in x.
  • The y-intercept is the predicted y when x is 0.
  • A point above the line means the actual value is greater than predicted.

Study design (heavily tested, rarely taught in CBSE)

The study has It allows
Random sample from a population Generalising to that population only
Random assignment to groups A cause-and-effect conclusion
Neither Only a statement about the people studied

Margin of error: the true value plausibly lies within the estimate plus or minus the margin. A larger sample gives a smaller margin.

Data practice

D1 (easy). Red and blue marbles are in the ratio 3:5. There are 40 marbles. How many are red?

D2 (easy). A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. At the same rate, how far does it travel in 4 hours?

D3 (medium). A price rises from $80 to $92. What is the percent increase?

D4 (medium). After a 25% discount, a jacket costs $60. What was the original price?

D5 (medium).

Tea Coffee Total
Grade 11 30 20 50
Grade 12 18 32 50
Total 48 52 100

One student who chose coffee is selected at random. What is the probability that the student is in Grade 12?

D6 (hard). A data set is 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. The value 13 is replaced by 33. Which is true?

  • A) The mean and the median both increase.
  • B) The mean increases and the median stays the same.
  • C) The mean stays the same and the median increases.
  • D) Neither changes.

D7 (hard). One hundred volunteers at a gym were randomly assigned to take a supplement or a placebo. The supplement group improved more on a strength test. Which conclusion is best supported?

  • A) The supplement improves strength for all adults.
  • B) The supplement caused the greater improvement among people like these volunteers.
  • C) No conclusion is possible because the volunteers were not a random sample.
  • D) The supplement is only associated with strength, not a cause of improvement.

D8 (hard). A train travels at 54 kilometres per hour. What is its speed in metres per second?

Geometry and Trigonometry

Mostly formula recall. The on-screen reference sheet gives areas, volumes and the special right triangles, but opening it costs time. Know these from memory.

Angles and lines

  • A straight line is 180 degrees. Angles in a triangle sum to 180.
  • Vertical angles are equal.
  • With parallel lines cut by a third line, every angle is one of two values that sum to 180.
  • Interior angles of a polygon with n sides sum to (n - 2) x 180.

Triangles

Fact Formula
Area (1/2) x base x height
Pythagorean theorem a2 + b2 = c2
Common triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and their multiples
45-45-90 triangle Sides x, x, x sqrt(2)
30-60-90 triangle Sides x, x sqrt(3), 2x
Similar triangles Sides in ratio k, areas in ratio k2

Traps. Using the slant side as the height. Matching the wrong pair of corresponding sides. Forgetting to square the scale factor for area.

Circles

Fact Formula
Circumference 2 pi r
Area pi r2
Arc length (angle / 360) x 2 pi r
Sector area (angle / 360) x pi r2
Equation (x - h)2 + (y - k)2 = r2, centre (h, k)
Radians pi radians = 180 degrees
  • A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
  • An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc.
  • To find the centre and radius from x2 + y2 + ax + by = c, complete the square, or type the equation into Desmos and read the graph.

Trap. The right-hand side is r2, not r.

Area and volume

Shape Volume
Rectangular box length x width x height
Cylinder pi r2 h
Cone (1/3) pi r2 h
Sphere (4/3) pi r3
Pyramid (1/3) x base area x height

If every length is multiplied by k, area is multiplied by k2 and volume by k3.

Coordinate geometry

  • Distance between two points: sqrt((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2).
  • Midpoint: average the x-values and average the y-values.

Right-triangle trigonometry

  • sin = opposite / hypotenuse. cos = adjacent / hypotenuse. tan = opposite / adjacent.
  • sin(x) = cos(90 - x). This identity appears regularly.
  • In similar right triangles, the trig ratios of matching angles are equal.
  • Given one ratio, draw the triangle, label two sides, and find the third with Pythagoras.

Desmos. Check the mode. Desmos defaults to radians. Switch to degrees with the wrench icon before typing sin(30).

CBSE note. Identities, heights and distances, and inverse trig are far beyond what is asked. Do not over-think these questions.

Geometry and Trig practice

E1 (easy). Two angles of a triangle measure 50 and 60 degrees. What is the third?

E2 (easy). A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. What is the hypotenuse?

E3 (medium). A circle has radius 6. What is the length of the arc cut off by a central angle of 60 degrees?

E4 (medium). sin(x) = cos(32 degrees), where x is between 0 and 90 degrees. What is x?

E5 (medium). A cylinder has radius 3 and height 8. What is its volume?

E6 (hard). In a right triangle, angle A is acute and tan A = 3/4. What is cos A?

E7 (hard). A circle has equation x2 + y2 + 6x - 8y = 0. What are its centre and radius?

E8 (hard). A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 10. What is its area?

E9 (hard). What is 5 pi / 6 radians in degrees?

Book 4

Desmos SAT Mastery

The rule for using Desmos

Desmos is a tool for about 8 to 12 of the 44 Math questions. It is built into Bluebook for the whole Math section. Practise only in the Bluebook version or at desmos.com/testing, so the buttons match test day.

The 10-second rule. If she can see the answer by hand in 10 seconds, do it by hand. If the algebra will take more than three lines, or the numbers are ugly, open Desmos.

Set-up habits

  • Keep the calculator open in a side panel for the whole section.
  • Delete old lines before each new question. Leftover graphs cause wrong clicks.
  • Use the wrench icon to set degrees before any trig.
  • If the graph is off screen, use the zoom buttons or the wrench to set the axes.
  • Type fractions with the / key and exponents with the ^ key.

The techniques

1. Systems of equations

Process. Type each equation on its own line, exactly as written. Click the point where the graphs cross.

Example. 3x + 4y = 26 and 5x - 2y = 0. What is x + y?

By hand. y = 2.5x, so 3x + 10x = 26, x = 2, y = 5. Answer 7. About 45 seconds.

Desmos. Two lines typed, one click: (2, 5). About 15 seconds.

Verdict. Desmos, unless the numbers are very simple.

2. Roots of a quadratic

Process. Type y = the expression. Click the points where the graph meets the x-axis.

Example. 2x2 - 7x - 15 = 0.

By hand. (2x + 3)(x - 5) = 0, so x = 5 or x = -1.5. About 50 seconds if the factoring is spotted.

Desmos. Type y = 2x2 - 7x - 15, click both intercepts. About 15 seconds.

Verdict. Desmos when a is not 1 or the roots are not whole numbers.

3. Maximum or minimum

Process. Graph the function. Click the turning point. Desmos shows its coordinates.

Example. h(t) = -5t2 + 30t + 2 gives the height of a ball. What is the maximum height?

By hand. t = -30 / (2 x -5) = 3. h(3) = -45 + 90 + 2 = 47.

Desmos. Type y = -5x2 + 30x + 2. Zoom out. Click the peak: (3, 47).

Verdict. About equal. Use Desmos to check. Read the question: it may ask for the time (3) or the height (47).

4. Any equation in one variable

Process. Type the left side as y = ... and the right side as y = ... on a second line. The x-coordinate of the intersection is the solution.

Example. 0.4x + 12 = 0.15x + 27.

By hand. 0.25x = 15, x = 60.

Desmos. Two lines, click the intersection at x = 60.

Verdict. By hand for simple linear equations. Desmos for equations with radicals, fractions or absolute values.

5. Exponential equations

Example. 500(1.08)t = 1000. After about how many years does the amount double?

By hand. Needs logarithms, which the SAT does not require.

Desmos. Type y = 500(1.08)x and y = 1000. Zoom out until both show. Intersection at x of about 9.

Verdict. Desmos, every time.

6. Sliders for unknown constants

Process. Type an equation containing a letter other than x or y. Desmos offers to add a slider. Drag it and watch the graph.

Example. For what value of c does x2 - 8x + c = 0 have exactly one solution?

By hand. 64 - 4c = 0, so c = 16. About 20 seconds if she knows the discriminant.

Desmos. Type y = x2 - 8x + c, add the slider, drag until the curve just touches the x-axis at c = 16.

Verdict. By hand if the discriminant is automatic. Slider as a check, or when the algebra is messy.

7. Checking equivalent expressions

Process. Type the original expression as y = ... Then type each answer choice. The correct choice draws exactly on top of the original.

Example. Which is equivalent to (x2 - 9) / (x - 3)? The graph matches y = x + 3.

Verdict. Desmos when the algebra is long. Faster still: plug x = 2 into the original and each choice by hand.

8. Evaluating functions

Process. Type f(x) = 3x2 - 2x + 1. On a new line type f(-2). Desmos shows 17.

Verdict. Desmos for f(g(x)) or awkward inputs. It prevents sign errors.

9. Tables

Process. Click the plus button and choose table. Enter x-values in the first column. Or type a function, then use the table to list its values.

Use. To check which equation matches a table in the question: enter the question's points in a table, then type each answer choice and see which graph passes through all the points.

Verdict. Desmos. This turns a medium question into a 30-second one.

10. Regression (line of best fit)

Process. Enter the data in a table with columns x1 and y1. On a new line type y1 ~ mx1 + b. Desmos reports m and b.

Example. Points (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 8), (4, 9) give m = 2.1 and b = 1.

Extra use. For a line through exactly two points, the regression gives the exact slope and intercept. For a quadratic through three points, type y1 ~ ax12 + bx1 + c.

Verdict. Desmos. There is no fast hand method.

11. Inequalities

Process. Type y > 2x - 1 and y < -x + 5. Desmos shades both. Solutions lie where the shading overlaps.

Example. Is (1, 2) a solution? Type the point (1, 2) and see whether it sits in the overlap. It does.

Verdict. By hand for testing one point. Desmos for "which graph" or "which point" questions with four choices.

12. Circles

Process. Type the equation as given, for example x2 + y2 + 6x - 8y = 0. Read the centre from the graph and count the radius.

Verdict. Desmos if completing the square is slow. By hand if it is automatic.

13. Statistics

Process. Type mean(4, 7, 7, 9, 13) or median(4, 7, 7, 9, 13).

Verdict. Desmos for lists of more than five numbers.

14. Word problems

Process. Translate into equations with x and y, then use technique 1.

Example. 150 tickets, adults $12, students $8, total $1,480. Type x + y = 150 and 12x + 8y = 1480. Intersection (70, 80).

Verdict. The translation is the hard part and Desmos cannot do it. Once the equations exist, Desmos is faster.

When not to use Desmos

Situation Why
One-step or two-step arithmetic and linear equations Typing is slower than thinking
"Which expression is equivalent" with easy factoring Pattern recognition takes 5 seconds
Interpretation questions ("what does 0.92 mean") Nothing to compute
Questions with several unknown constants A graph cannot be drawn
Geometry with a diagram Formula recall is faster
Study design and statistics reasoning No calculation

Common Desmos mistakes

  • Reading the y-coordinate when x was asked.
  • Missing a second intersection that is off screen. Always zoom out once.
  • Radians when the question is in degrees.
  • Typing 2x2-7x-15 without parentheses around a negative input, such as -32 instead of (-3)2.
  • Trusting a rounded decimal when the answer choices are fractions. Convert with the fraction button.

Daily 5-minute drill

From Day 3 onward, do three of the techniques above each day from memory, timed. By October 24 each one should take under 20 seconds.

Book 5

SAT Practice Questions

How to use this bank

These 34 original questions are sorted by difficulty. With the diagnostic and the practice sets in Books 2 and 3, the system holds about 130 original questions. For volume beyond that, use the College Board Student Question Bank, which has thousands of official questions filterable by skill and difficulty.

Level Meaning Target accuracy for 1400 Time per question
1. Foundation Easy questions from Module 1 100% Under 45 sec
2. Medium The bulk of both modules 95% Under 70 sec
3. Hard The hard end of Module 1, much of the harder Module 2 75% Under 100 sec
4. 1400+ challenge The hardest questions in the harder Module 2 50% Up to 2 min, or flag

Do each level timed. Mark every answer S, U or G. Check the key only after finishing the level. A miss at Level 1 or 2 is more serious than a miss at Level 4.

Level 1 key

Q Answer Skill Explanation and why the others are wrong Fastest method Common trap
1.1 B Words in context First-time users had no difficulty, so the instructions were easy to follow. Vague is the opposite. Lengthy and technical would make it harder. Read the result clause, predict "easy" Picking a word that describes instructions in general
1.2 C Possessive pronoun The experiment belongs to the students. "There" is a place, "they're" is "they are", "theirs" cannot come before a noun. Substitute "they are". If it fails, it is not they're. Choosing by sound
1.3 D Transition Rain forecast caused the move. However is contrast, for example and similarly do not show cause. Test "so" in the gap Reading only the second sentence
1.4 A Sentence boundary Complete sentence, then an explanation. B is a comma splice, C is a run-on, D adds a stray comma. Check both sides for subject and verb Comma splice
1.5 6 Linear equation 4x = 24. By hand Arithmetic slip
1.6 7 Function value 3(4) - 5. By hand Subtracting before multiplying
1.7 75 Percent 0.3 x 250. By hand Dividing instead of multiplying
1.8 13 Pythagoras 5-12-13 triple. Recognise the triple Adding the sides

Q Answer Skill Explanation and why the others are wrong Fastest method Common trap
2.1 A Detail Stated directly: glucose "prevents ice from forming inside" the cells. B contradicts "freezing solid". C and D are never mentioned. Find the word glucose, read that sentence B, which sounds right but reverses the text
2.2 B Subject-verb agreement Subject is "series", singular. A, C and D are plural forms. Cross out "of experiments conducted by the graduate students" Matching the verb to "students"
2.3 D Notes Only D names something both share. A and C cover one instrument. B gives a difference. Read the goal, look for "both" Choosing an accurate but off-goal sentence
2.4 C Nonessential phrase The description needs a comma on both sides. A leaves it open. B splits "geologist and cartographer". D uses a semicolon before an incomplete clause. Removal test Forgetting the closing comma
2.5 3 System Add the equations: 3x = 12, x = 4, so y = 3. Elimination or Desmos Answering 4 (that is x)
2.6 B Quadratic (x + 8)(x - 2) = 0. Solutions -8 and 2. Plug in the choices Sign error giving -2 or 8
2.7 $35.70 Percent 40 x 0.85 = 34. 34 x 1.05 = 35.70. Multiply the two multipliers Subtracting 10% in one step ($36)
2.8 27 Similar triangles 6/4 = h/18. Proportion Inverting the ratio (12)
